Question #1

You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline. Both approaches produce the same kind of object. In your own words, explain why data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length, and what error you would expect if they didn’t.

  A data frame represents a rectangular table where every row corresponds to a single observation or record across all columns. If the column arguments had different lengths, the rows would be incomplete or misaligned, making it impossible to form a valid table. If you pass vectors of unequal lengths into data.frame(), R will stop and throw an error message stating that the arguments imply a differing number of rows (unless the shorter vector's length divides evenly into the longer one, in which case R recycles the values).


Question #2

A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.”
Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?

  This description makes sense because a list in R is flexible and can store different types of objects as separate elements, which allows each column in a data frame to hold a different data type such as character, numeric, or logical. However, each individual column inside that list is an atomic vector, and atomic vectors can only store elements of a single, uniform data type.

Question #3

students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects. Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.

```{r}

class(students["age"])
class(students$age)

```

  When you run class(students["age"]), R returns "data.frame", whereas running class(students$age) returns "numeric". Just like using single brackets [ ] on a list returns a smaller sub-list, using single brackets on a data frame preserves the outer container structure and returns a one-column data frame. In contrast, using $ (or double brackets [[ ]]) extracts the raw element stored inside that position, giving you a plain numeric vector.


Question #4

In df-multiple-conditions, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19) before that combined result is used to filter rows. What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

  The & operator compares the two logical vectors element by element and produces a single combined logical vector that is TRUE only at positions where both conditions are TRUE for the same student. If you used | (OR) instead of & (AND), the combined vector would be TRUE whenever at least one of the conditions is met, which would return more rows—including students who passed even if they are 19 or younger, as well as students older than 19 even if they failed.

Question #5

Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name). Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.

```{r}

summary(students)

```

  For the numeric column (age), R produces a statistical summary containing the minimum, first quartile, median, mean, third quartile, and maximum values. For the logical column (passed), R displays the mode alongside the exact counts of TRUE and FALSE entries. For the character column (name), R simply reports the total length (number of elements), the class, and the mode, because calculating an average or mean requires numbers and makes no mathematical sense for text labels like names.


Question #6

str() and summary() both describe a data frame, but they show different information. Based on what you observed, when would str() be more useful to you than summary(), and vice versa?

  The str() function is more useful when you want to inspect the technical layout of a data frame, such as checking the exact dimensions, verifying each column's data type, and previewing the first few actual values. On the other hand, summary() is more useful when you want to analyze the distribution of your data, check the range of numeric values, or see category counts across the entire dataset.

Question #7

After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from df-logical-filter (students$passed == TRUE)? Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.

  No, I could not run that filter anymore because the passed column is already gone from the students data frame. When I try to run students$passed == TRUE, R returns an empty logical vector (logical(0)), which gives a data frame with zero rows instead of filtering the students. Keeping track of the data frame's current structure matters because the next steps in my code depend on the columns that are still there, and deleting a column too early will break any code that needs it later on.



Question #8

order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions. Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).

  First, order(students$age) checks the values in the age column and finds their row numbers from the youngest to the oldest, returning a vector of row positions (3, 1, 5, 2, 4). Next, putting that vector before the comma inside students[ , ] tells R to pick the rows in that exact new order. Finally, leaving the space after the comma blank tells R to include all columns for those rows, so the whole data frame gets sorted together.

Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge.

grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

TODO: Add a new column "average" to grades that holds the mean of midterm and final for each student. Hint: (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2.

```{r}

grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

```

Question #9

Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?”.

  Based on the data frame, a consistently low midterm score seems more responsible for a student's final remark because a student who starts with a very low midterm grade has a much harder time reaching a passing average even if their final exam score improves.


Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.

  First, I would add a new column to the grades data frame that subtracts the midterm score from the final score (grades$final - grades$midterm) so I can see if each student's grade went up or down. Second, I would subset the grades data frame to separate the students who failed (grades$remarks == "Failed") from the students who passed (grades$remarks == "Passed") so I can compare the two groups easily. Third, I would sort the failed group by their midterm scores and then by their new score-difference column using order() to see whether most failing students started with low midterm grades or had a large drop on the final exam.


----------------------------------------------------------------------
CONCLUSION.

  A data frame is R’s main table structure that organizes data into rows and columns. It is essentially a list of equal-length vectors, where each vector acts as a column that can store a different data type while keeping all values inside that single column the same type. Because real-world datasets usually combine different types of information like text, numbers, and logical values in one table, data frames are the most practical structure for data analysis in R.
